frequency_question: How often does structural and diplomatic friction prevent the actual imposition of threatened secondary sanctions against major tier-1 foreign banks?
membership_rule: Includes formal public warnings or statutory deadlines targeting systemically important foreign commercial banks for purchasing restricted crude oil, where waiver authorities or diplomatic off-ramps were available. Excludes minor non-systemic institutions and non-energy secondary sanctions.

cases.name: NDAA 2012 / Iran Sanctions Act implementation against Chinese banks
CAATSA Section 231 threats against major international buyers of Russian/Iranian defense or energy
Maximum Pressure campaign waiver non-renewals against Chinese state refiners/banks
Post-2022 Russian oil price cap enforcement threats against intermediary Chinese/Indian banks

provenance_note: rate of 0% from only 4 case(s); too few to establish an extreme base rate -- treat as directional
coverage_note: 4 named major historical friction cycles representing the modern era of energy-related secondary banking threats.
known_gaps: Excludes minor Tier-3 or rural Chinese banks occasionally hit with lesser administrative frictions.
skeleton: Total high-level diplomatic confrontations over systemic secondary banking sanctions for energy purchases vs. actual executions resulting in SWIFT/financial system cutoffs of major tier-1 banks.
multiplier: 4 attempted pressure campaigns divided by 0 successful executions of terminal secondary sanctions on major tier-1 Chinese commercial banks.
validity_reason: The structural friction model relies on systemic macroeconomic interdependence between the US and Chinese banking sectors, which changes slowly over multi-year periods.
